claim: Social learning is defined as acquiring new knowledge through observing or directly interacting with others and is a fundamental behavior of humans and animals.
source: Social learning, defined as acquiring new knowledge through observing or directly interacting with others, is a fundamental behavior of humans and animals (Bandura, 1997; Meltzoff et al., 2009; Heyes and Galef, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on social learning.

claim: Humans and some primates employ imitation learning.
source: Besides the imitation learning that humans and some primates employ (Bandura, 1997; Meltzoff et al., 2009; Zentall, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Social facilitation or local enhancement is a common behavioral effect in many animal species.
source: a common behavioral effect in many animal species is the so-called 'social facilitation' (Zentall, 2006; Zentall and Levine, 1972; Zajonc, 1965) or 'local enhancement' (Heyes and Galef, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An animal's understanding of an environment is facilitated by the presence of other social subjects in the same environment.
source: an animal's understanding of an environment is facilitated by the presence of other social subjects in the same environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the surrounding context.

claim: Local enhancement can be caused by enhanced sensory processing due to heightened attention, acquiring environmental attributes such as safety or food availability, or other unspecified means.
source: Local enhancement can be caused possibly by enhanced sensory processing due to heightened attention, acquiring environmental attributes such as safety or food availability, or other unspecified means (Heyes and Galef, 1996; Zentall, 2006; Zajonc, 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The presence of social subjects in an environment impacts other animals' neural processing of information related to the environment.
source: According to this idea, the presence of social subjects in an environment impacts other animals' neural processing of information related to the environment.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the local enhancement theory described in the cited literature.

claim: Spatial information of an environment is represented in spatial memory by hippocampal place cells in humans and rodents.
source: In humans and rodents, spatial information of an environment is represented in spatial memory by hippocampal place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational research on place cells.

claim: Hippocampal place cells fire at specific locations (place fields) of a given environment.
source: hippocampal place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993), which fire at specific locations (place fields) of a given environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational research on place cells.

claim: When a rat travels along a linear track from one end to the other, a subset of place cells display place fields on the track and they fire one after another in a unique sequence.
source: For example, when a rat travels along a linear track from one end to the other, a subset of place cells display place fields on the track and they fire one after another in a unique sequence (Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When an animal explores a different environment such as an open box, hippocampal place cells 'remap'.
source: When the animal explores a different environment such as an open box, hippocampal place cells 'remap' (Leutgeb et al., 2005; Colgin et al., 2008; Alme et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During remapping, place cells either alter firing locations, stop firing, or become active.
source: hippocampal place cells 'remap' (Leutgeb et al., 2005; Colgin et al., 2008; Alme et al., 2014), i.e., they either alter firing locations, stop firing, or become active.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nine Long-Evans rats (4–6 months old, male) were implanted with a hyperdrive containing 15 independently movable tetrodes and a reference electrode, targeting the right dorsal hippocampal CA1 region.
source: Nine Long-Evans rats (4–6 months old, male) were implanted with a hyperdrive that contained 15 independently movable tetrodes and a reference electrode, targeting the right dorsal hippocampal CA1 region (coordinates: anteroposterior −3.8 mm, mediolateral 2.4 mm relative to Bregma).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: A total of 3290 putative pyramidal CA1 cells were recorded from all animals on all recording days.
source: A total of 3290 putative pyramidal CA1 cells (defined as mean firing rate < 6 Hz) were recorded from all animals on all recording days.
evidence: The claim reports the number of cells recorded in the experiment.

claim: 2200 cells were active (with mean rate > 0.5 Hz) in at least one of the Pre-box, Track, and Post-box sessions on a given recording day.
source: Here we analyzed 2200 cells that were active (with mean rate > 0.5 Hz) in at least one of the Pre-box, Track, and Post-box sessions on a given recording day.
evidence: The claim reports the number of cells analyzed in the study.

claim: On average, the animals spent about 53% of the time facing the opening side of the box.
source: On average, the animals spent about 53% of the time facing the opening side of the box.
evidence: The claim reports a behavioral measurement from the experiment.

claim: The percentage of time animals spent facing the opening side of the box did not differ among different box conditions, except for the Blocked-view condition.
source: However, this percentage did not differ among different box conditions (Figure 1C), except for the Blocked-view condition, where the opening side was blocked and rats predictably spent less percentage of time facing the opening side.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: On average, 18.7 ± 1.1 rotation events were identified per session.
source: On average, 18.7 ± 1.1 rotation events were identified per session
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of rotation events among different box conditions or between Pre- and Post-box.
source: there was no significant difference among different box conditions or between Pre- and Post-box (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis.

claim: The rotation events lasted for an average of 6.67 ± 0.05 s.
source: The rotation events lasted for an average of 6.67 ± 0.05 s.
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: Rotation events were accompanied by strong theta (6–10 Hz) oscillations without much high-frequency (100–250 Hz) sharp-wave ripples.
source: Analysis of CA1 local field potentials (LFPs) shows that rotation events were accompanied by strong theta (6–10 Hz) oscillations (Buzsáki, 2002) without much high-frequency (100–250 Hz) sharp-wave ripples (Buzsáki et al., 1992) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by LFP analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Theta is commonly associated with active behavior such as maze-running whereas ripples mostly occur during inactive behavior such as immobility or slow-wave sleep.
source: Since theta is commonly associated with active behavior such as maze-running whereas ripples mostly occur during inactive behavior such as immobility or slow-wave sleep (Buzsáki, 2002; Buzsáki et al., 1992)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hippocampus was in an active state during rotation events.
source: the analysis indicates that the hippocampus was in an active state during rotation events.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the LFP analysis showing theta oscillations during rotation events.

claim: On average, 14.7 ± 0.4 rotation-active cells were identified per session.
source: We identified those CA1 cells that were active in rotation events (14.7 ± 0.4 rotation-active cells per session)
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: 40% of rotation-active CA1 cells (566 out of 1421) were significantly tuned to head direction during rotation events in the box.
source: We found that 40% of rotation-active CA1 cells (566 out of 1421) were significantly tuned to head direction during rotation events in the box (p<0.05, Rayleigh test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: 74% of rotation-active cells were rotation-consistent.
source: We found that 74% of rotation-active cells were rotation-consistent.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of rotation consistency.

claim: On average, 10.2 ± 0.5 location-consistent cells were identified per box session.
source: On average, we identified 10.2 ± 0.5 location-consistent cells per box session.
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: The average rotation-consistency within CW or CCW events was significantly greater than that across CW and CCW rotation events of same sessions.
source: First, we found that the average rotation-consistency within CW or CCW events was significantly greater than that across CW and CCW rotation events of same sessions (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and statistical analysis.

claim: 42% of rotation-consistent cells (29% of all rotation-active cells) were also consistent between CW and CCW events.
source: Nevertheless, 42% of rotation-consistent cells (29% of all rotation-active cells) were also consistent between CW and CCW events.
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: The rotation-consistency was similar among different box conditions.
source: Second, the rotation-consistency was similar among different box conditions (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and statistical analysis.

claim: On average, there were 18.8 ± 0.9 laps per trajectory per track session.
source: On average, there were 18.8 ± 0.9 laps per trajectory per track session
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: Each lap lasted for 5.8 ± 0.2 s.
source: each lap lasted for 5.8 ± 0.2 s.
evidence: The claim reports a measurement from the experiment.

claim: Among the 2200 cells active either during rotation in the box or during lap-running on the track across all days, 601 cells were active only during rotation, 779 cells only during lap-running, and 820 cells (common cells) during both rotation and lap running on at least one track trajectory.
source: Among the 2200 cells active either during rotation in the box or during lap-running on the track across all days, 601 cells were active only during rotation, 779 cells only during lap-running, and 820 cells (common cells) during both rotation and lap running on at least one track trajectory (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim reports the distribution of cell activity from the experiment.

claim: Overall, 58% of all rotation-active cells and 51% of all running-active cells were common cells.
source: These numbers indicate that, overall, 58% of all rotation-active cells and 51% of all running-active cells were common cells.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the data reported in the manuscript.

claim: In the Trained-demo and Naïve-demo sessions combined, the proportions of common cells (69% of all rotation-active cells, 58% of all running-active cells) were significantly higher than those in other box sessions combined (48% of all rotation-active cells, 44% of all running-active cells).
source: However, we found that, in the Trained-demo and Naïve-demo sessions combined, these proportions of common cells (69% of all rotation-active cells, 58% of all running-active cells) were significantly higher than those in other (Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, Blocked-view) box sessions combined (48% of all rotation-active cells, p=3.4 × 10–21, binomial test comparing with that of Trained- and Naïve-demo combined; 44% of all running-active cells, p=7.5 × 10–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Many active CA1 cells were 'cross-activated' between the box and the track in the presence of a demonstrator, either well-trained or naïve.
source: This finding suggests that many active CA1 cells were 'cross-activated' between the box and the track in the presence of a demonstrator, either well-trained or naïve.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on common cells.

claim: The actual proportion of common cells was significantly higher than the chance proportion for the Trained-demo and Naïve-demo sessions, but not for others (Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, Blocked-view).
source: We found that the actual proportion was significantly higher than the chance proportion for the Trained-demo and Naïve-demo sessions, but not for others (Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, Blocked-view) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: The PDI was significantly greater in the Trained- and Naïve-demo sessions than other sessions.
source: Similarly, the PDI was significantly greater in the Trained- and Naïve-demo sessions than other sessions (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: As long as and only when a demonstrator was present, was there cross-activation of CA1 cells significantly more than the chance level between the box and the track.
source: This analysis indicates that, as long as and only when a demonstrator was present, was there cross-activation of CA1 cells significantly more than the chance level between the box and the track.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on common cells and PDI.

claim: 125 out of 639 (20%) rotation sequences under Trained-demo and 73 out of 336 (22%) rotation sequences under Naïve-demo were matching sequences.
source: We found that 125 out of 639 (20%) rotation sequences under Trained-demo and 73 out of 336 (22%) rotation sequences under Naïve-demo were matching sequences.
evidence: The claim reports the results of sequence matching analysis.

claim: Only 73 out of 712 (10%), 13 out of 116 (11%), 42 out of 419 (10%), and 22 out of 314 (7%) of rotation sequences under Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, and Blocked-view were matching sequences, respectively.
source: In contrast, only 73 out of 712 (10%), 13 out of 116 (11%), 42 out of 419 (10%), and 22 out of 314 (7%) of rotation sequences under Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, and Blocked-view were matching sequences, respectively.
evidence: The claim reports the results of sequence matching analysis.

claim: The actual number of matching sequences was significant under Trained-demo and Naïve-demo, but not under Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, or Blocked-view.
source: Relative to the shuffle-generated distribution of number of matching sequences, we found that the actual number of matching sequences was significant under Trained-demo and Naïve-demo, but not under Empty-track, No-track, Toy-car, or Blocked-view (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and statistical analysis.

claim: A significant number of matching sequences was found consistently in 8 out of the 8 rats that yielded sufficient cells for the analysis.
source: We found a significant number of matching sequences consistently in 8 out of the 8 rats that yielded sufficient cells for the analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Firing sequences of common cells were preserved between lap-running and rotation events under Trained-demo and Naïve-demo conditions.
source: Therefore, our analysis indicates that firing sequences of common cells were preserved between lap-running and rotation events under Trained-demo and Naïve-demo conditions.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the sequence matching analysis.

claim: The precise firing times of common cells were not preserved.
source: Further analysis found that the precise firing times of common cells were not preserved (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Firing sequences of multiple common cells during lap-running were cross-activated in a significant number of rotation events in the box, but only when a demonstrator was present.
source: The results nevertheless indicate that firing sequences of multiple common cells during lap-running were cross-activated in a significant number of rotation events in the box, but only when a demonstrator was present.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the sequence matching analysis.

claim: The actual proportion of common cells was significantly greater than the chance proportion only under Trained-demo, not under Empty-track, in Pre-box on the first recording day before rats ran the track themselves for the very first time.
source: We found that the actual proportion of common cells was significantly greater than the chance proportion only under Trained-demo, not under Empty-track (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and statistical analysis.

claim: The actual number of matching sequences was significantly greater than the chance level only under Trained-demo, not under Empty-track, in Pre-box on the first recording day before rats ran the track themselves for the very first time.
source: Second, the actual number of matching sequences was also significantly greater than the chance level only under Trained-demo, not under Empty-track (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and statistical analysis.

claim: Cross-activation of the track-running CA1 activity was present in the box session prior to any self-running experience, but only when a demonstrator was present.
source: These results suggest that cross-activation of the track-running CA1 activity was present in the box session prior to any self-running experience, but only when a demonstrator was present.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on common cells and matching sequences before first self-running experience.

claim: Actual proportion of common cells was similar to the chance proportion in rest sessions.
source: We found that actual proportion of common cells was similar to the chance proportion (Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: The actual number of matching sequences was not significantly greater than the chance level in rest sessions.
source: the actual number of matching sequences was not significantly greater than the chance level (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and statistical analysis.

claim: Cross-activation was unique to the box that had an opening to the nearby track where a demonstrator was present.
source: The analysis suggests that cross-activation was unique to the box that had an opening to the nearby track where a demonstrator was present.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data comparing the small box with the rest box.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of common cells between Pre-box and Post-box on the first and second day of recording under Trained-demo or Naïve-demo.
source: We found no significant difference in the proportion of common cells between Pre-box and Post-box (using PDI as a measure, Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and statistical analysis.

claim: The actual number of matching sequences was significantly greater than the chance level in both Pre-box and Post-box on the first and second day of recording under Trained-demo or Naïve-demo.
source: The actual number of matching sequences was significantly greater than the chance level in both Pre-box and Post-box (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and statistical analysis.

claim: The cross-activation in Pre- and Post-box was largely similar.
source: The data thus suggest that the cross-activation in Pre- and Post-box was largely similar.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data comparing Pre-box and Post-box.

claim: The cross-activation was largely similar between Day1 and Day2.
source: We found that the cross-activation was also largely similar between Day1 and Day2 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: Cross-activation of CA1 activity was insensitive to animals' self-experience on the track.
source: These results suggest that cross-activation of CA1 activity was insensitive to animals' self-experience on the track.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data comparing Pre-box vs Post-box and Day1 vs Day2.

claim: Both mean running speed and number of running laps per trajectory in the Trained-demo rats were significantly greater than those in the Empty-track rats on both Day1 and Day2.
source: Both parameters in the Trained-demo rats were significantly greater than those in the Empty-track rats on both Day1 and Day2 (Figure 8A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and statistical analysis.

claim: There was an improvement in track running performance in the Trained-demo rats compared to Empty-track rats.
source: suggesting an improvement in track running performance in the former group.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Spatial information of cells in the Trained-demo rats were significantly greater than those in the Empty-track rats on both Day1 and Day2.
source: Indeed, spatial information of cells in the Trained-demo rats were significantly greater than those in the Empty-track rats on both Day1 and Day2 (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and statistical analysis.

claim: The improvement in spatial information was small on Day1 (15% increase in median spatial information from Empty-track to Trained-demo) and became modest on Day2 (38%).
source: This improvement in spatial information was small on Day1 (15% increase in median spatial information from Empty-track to Trained-demo) and became modest on Day2 (38%).
evidence: The claim reports the magnitude of improvement in spatial information.

claim: Lap consistency of cells in the Trained-demo rats appeared greater than those in the Empty-track rats, but did not reach statistical significance.
source: Lap consistency of cells in the Trained-demo rats also appeared greater than those in the Empty-track rats, but did not reach statistical significance (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a mild speedup in novel place field development in the Trained-demo rats.
source: The result suggests a mild speedup in novel place field development in the Trained-demo rats.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the place field analysis.

claim: Cross-activation was accompanied by an improvement in track-running performance and place field development.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that cross-activation was accompanied by an improvement in track-running performance and place field development.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral and place field data.

claim: The number of ripple events per unit time was slightly, but significantly increased from Pre-box (0.28 ± 0.03 ripples/s) to Post-box (0.31 ± 0.02 ripples/s) sessions.
source: We found that the number of ripple events per unit time was slightly, but significantly increased from Pre-box (0.28 ± 0.03 ripples/s) to Post-box (0.31 ± 0.02 ripples/s) sessions (t = 2.7, p=0.009, paired t-test; N = 72 sessions with all conditions combined).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The number of ripples was not significantly different across different conditions in either Pre-box or Post-box.
source: However, the number of ripples was not significantly different across different conditions in either Pre-box (F(5,66)= 2.0, p=0.09, One-way ANOVA) or Post-box (F(5,66) = 1.9, p=0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: A significant number of replay events was found under all box conditions with Pre-box and Post-box sessions combined.
source: First, with Pre-box and Post-box sessions combined, we found a significant number of replay events under all conditions (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9B and statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of replay events among all candidate events was 7.7% under Trained-demo, 12.5% under Naïve-demo, 7.8% under Empty-track, 14.6% under No-track, 9.3% under Toy-car, and 11.2% under Blocked-view.
source: The percentage of replay events among all candidate events was 7.7% under Trained-demo, 12.5% under Naïve-demo, 7.8% under Empty-track, 14.6% under No-track, 9.3% under Toy-car, and 11.2% under Blocked-view.
evidence: The claim reports the results of replay analysis.

claim: Ripple-associated replay occurred in the box, consistent with the previously found 'remote replay', but the replay was comparable with or without a demonstrator.
source: The result suggests that ripple-associated replay occurred in the box, consistent with the previously found 'remote replay' (Karlsson and Frank, 2009), but the replay was comparable with or without a demonstrator.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data and is supported by a citation.

claim: The number of replay events was significant in Post-box (9.2%), but did not reach the statistical significance in Pre-box (6.7%).
source: We found that the number of replay events was significant in Post-box (9.2%), but did not reach the statistical significance in Pre-box (6.7%)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Direct track experience enhanced ripple-associated replay.
source: suggesting that direct track experience enhanced ripple-associated replay.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data comparing Pre-box and Post-box.

claim: None of the number of replay events in Pre-box and Post-box on the first day under Trained-demo and Empty-track reached the statistical significant level.
source: Under both conditions, although there appeared an increase in replay from Pre-box (Trained-demo: 4.7%; Empty-track: 4.7%) to Post-box Trained-demo: 7.7%; Empty-track: 6.8%), none of the number of replay events reached the statistical significant level (Figure 9D)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and statistical analysis.

claim: There was absence of replay before the first track running experience and weak replay after.
source: suggesting the absence of replay before the first track running experience and weak replay after.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data on the first day.

claim: In contrast to the matching sequences within rotation events, ripple-associated replay was experience-dependent and was not specific to the presence of a demonstrator.
source: Our data are thus consistent with the idea that, in contrast to the matching sequences within rotation events, ripple-associated replay was experience-dependent and was not specific to the presence of a demonstrator.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data.

claim: The mean z-scored spatial information and lap-consistency of all active cells under either Trained-demo or Naïve-demo were not significantly different from the chance level of 0.
source: The mean z-scored spatial information and lap-consistency of all active cells under either Trained-demo or Naïve-demo were not significantly different from the chance level of 0 (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10B,C and statistical analysis.

claim: 0.6% of cells in the Trained-demo rats and 0.4% in the Naïve-demo rats had significant spatial information.
source: We found that 0.6% of cells in the Trained-demo rats and 0.4% in the Naïve-demo rats had significant spatial information (Z > 1.645, p<0.05)
evidence: The claim reports the results of spatial information analysis.

claim: 0% of cells in the Trained-demo rats and 0% in the Naïve-demo rats had significant lap consistency.
source: 0% of cells in the Trained-demo rats and 0% in the Naïve-demo rats had significant lap consistency.
evidence: The claim reports the results of lap consistency analysis.

claim: The data did not support the idea that CA1 cells in the box respond to the demonstrator's positions on the track.
source: Therefore, our data did not support the idea that CA1 cells in the box respond to the demonstrator's positions on the track.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the spatial tuning analysis.

claim: CA1 cells formed consistent firing sequences during rotation events in the box.
source: We found that CA1 cells formed consistent firing sequences during rotation events in the box.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on rotation-consistent cells.

claim: A group of CA1 cells (common cells) were active during both rotation events in the box and lap-running events on the track with similar firing patterns.
source: A group of these cells (common cells) were also active during lap-running events on the track with similar firing patterns, as shown by similar multi-cell firing sequences across rotation and lap-running events.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on common cells.

claim: Cross-activation was specific to the box and took place only when a demonstrator (either Trained-demo or Naive-demo) was present on the track.
source: This cross-activation was specific to the box and took place only when a demonstrator (either Trained-demo or Naive-demo) was present on the track.
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on cross-activation.

claim: The cross-activation appeared before the animals' very first running experience on the track, as well as after the experience.
source: Importantly, the cross-activation appeared before the animals' very first running experience on the track, as well as after the experience
evidence: The claim summarizes the findings on experience-independence of cross-activation.

claim: Place cell activities representing a track can be activated by staying in a separate, nearby box while another rat running on the track.
source: Our data thus show that place cell activities representing a track can be activated by staying in a separate, nearby box while another rat running on the track.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Presence of social subjects in an environment can enhance the activation of an observer's hippocampal place cell activity patterns that encode the environment.
source: This finding supports our hypothesis that presence of social subjects in an environment can enhance the activation of an observer's hippocampal place cell activity patterns that encode the environment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the main finding in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: Place cells are tuned to specific locations within a small space in active behavior and they fire with a sequence when the animal actively moves his head along a trajectory.
source: This implies that, even if an animal is confined to a small space, place cells are tuned to specific locations within the space in active behavior and they fire with a sequence when the animal actively moves his head along a trajectory.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the firing sequences during rotation events.

claim: Place fields shrink as the animal's space shrinks.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the well-known phenomenon that place fields shrink as the animal's space shrinks (Gothard et al., 1996; O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cross-activation is partial, that is, only for a set of common cells, not all place cells active on the track or in the box.
source: However, we need to point out that this cross-activation is partial, that is, only for a set of common cells, not all place cells active on the track or in the box.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on common cells.

claim: Common cells comprise about 58% of place cells on the track under Trained-demo or Naive-demo condition and about 20% of the sequences of these cells during rotation events matched with the track templates.
source: In fact, common cells comprise about 58% of place cells on the track under Trained-demo or Naive-demo condition and about 20% of the sequences of these cells during rotation events matched with the track templates.
evidence: The claim reports the proportions of common cells and matching sequences.

claim: The overall spatial presentations of the track and the box remain relatively separated.
source: In any case, our data means that the overall spatial presentations of the track and the box remain relatively separated.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the partial cross-activation.

claim: A significant number of firing patterns are common in both presentations.
source: However, a significant number of firing patterns are common in both presentations.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on common cells and matching sequences.

claim: There exist common firing motifs consisting of a subset of place cells that can be activated in different environments or in different behavior.
source: This finding suggests the existence of common firing motifs consisting of a subset of place cells that can be activated in different environments or in different behavior (Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data and is supported by a citation.

claim: The presence of social subjects can enhance the cross-activation of such common firing motifs of place cells across different environments.
source: Importantly, our results reveal that the presence of social subjects can enhance the cross-activation of such common firing motifs of place cells across different environments.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the main finding.

claim: Cross-activation shows little experience-dependence, suggesting that it may be driven by sensory cues rather than experience.
source: The fact that cross-activation shows little experience-dependence suggests that it may be driven by sensory cues rather than experience.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experience-independence of cross-activation.

claim: Common external input biases common motifs to emerge in both environments.
source: It is possible that this common external input biases common motifs to emerge in both environments.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism of cross-activation.

claim: The initiation of common firing motifs could be triggered by common external visual cues.
source: Interestingly, the rats' rotation events consistently started and ended at the opening side, consistent with this idea that the initiation of common firing motifs could be triggered by common external visual cues.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the behavioral observation.

claim: Under the Blocked-view condition where there was a demonstrator on the track but external room cues and the demonstrator were invisible to the rat in the small box, cross-activation did not occur, supporting a crucial role of common visual cues in cross-activation.
source: Furthermore, under the Blocked-view condition where there was a demonstrator on the track but external room cues and the demonstrator were invisible to the rat in the small box, cross-activation did not occur, supporting a crucial role of common visual cues in cross-activation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data from the Blocked-view condition.

claim: The cross-activation of track templates during rotation events suggests a topological similarity between firing motifs representing the track-running trajectories and the head movement trajectories in the box.
source: According to our interpretation that the firing of CA1 cells during rotation mainly results from 'squeezed' place cell activity, the cross-activation of track templates during rotation events suggests a topological similarity between firing motifs representing the track-running trajectories and the head movement trajectories in the box.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the cross-activation phenomenon.

claim: Place cell patterns may encode common topology in seemingly very different environments.
source: This is consistent with the proposal that place cell patterns may encode common topology in seemingly very different environments (Dabaghian et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When there is a demonstrator moving on the track, the rat in the box may 'realize' that the track is another space within the same room that can be explored.
source: When there is a demonstrator moving on the track, the rat in the box may 'realize' that the track is another space within the same room that can be explored.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism of cross-activation.

claim: This sense of track as an explorable space might bias the drive to a subset of place cells in both the box and the track toward shared distal room cues, and lead to the emergence of common firing motifs and thus cross-activation.
source: This sense of track as an explorable space might bias the drive to a subset of place cells in both the box and the track toward shared distal room cues, and lead to the emergence of common firing motifs and thus cross-activation.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism of cross-activation.

claim: Cross-activation does not require precise behavioral performance of the demonstrator.
source: Interestingly, our data show that both a well-trained and a naive demonstrator are capable of triggering cross-activation, which suggests that cross-activation does not require precise behavioral performance of the demonstrator.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data comparing Trained-demo and Naïve-demo conditions.

claim: The rat in the box may not necessarily understand the precise action of the demonstrator, but the presence of the demonstrator itself is sufficient to signal the spatial nature of the track.
source: Therefore, the rat in the box may not necessarily understand the precise action of the demonstrator, but the presence of the demonstrator itself is sufficient to signal the spatial nature of the track (instead of merely a visual cue in the room), which leads to the cross-activation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data on cross-activation.

claim: Animals can learn about an environment, without actual self-exploration.
source: In this way, animals can learn about an environment, without actual self-exploration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the cross-activation phenomenon.

claim: Rodents can learn a variety of tasks by observing a conspecific.
source: Indeed, it is known that rodents can learn a variety of tasks by observing a conspecific (Zentall and Levine, 1972; Leggio et al., 2000; Jeon et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rodents rely on local enhancement or social facilitation as a general scheme of social learning.
source: One theory is that, instead of imitation learning that requires detailed understanding of conspecifics' actions, rodents rely on local enhancement or social facilitation as a general scheme of social learning (Heyes and Galef, 1996; Zentall, 2006; Zajonc, 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The finding that cross-activation can be facilitated by both trained and naïve conspecifics is consistent with the local enhancement theory.
source: Our finding that cross-activation can be facilitated by both trained and naïve conspecifics is consistent with the local enhancement theory
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data in relation to the local enhancement theory.

claim: The finding may provide a specific neural mechanism of local enhancement in social learning.

evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: Social observation facilitates the development of novel place fields.
source: More interestingly, their place fields during the first a few laps on the track seem already better tuned, suggesting that social observation facilitates the development of novel place fields.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the place field data.

claim: It is possible that the facilitation of place field development is related to the cross-activation in the box.
source: It is possible that this facilitation is related to the cross-activation in the box.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relationship between cross-activation and place field development.

claim: Ripple replay does not occur in the box before the first self-running on the track and are similar across various box conditions in our experiment.
source: Although ripple-associated replay may or may not take place prior to experience in other tasks (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013; Silva et al., 2015), ripple replay does not occur in the box before the first self-running on the track and are similar across various box conditions in our experiment.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data and is supported by citations.

claim: Ripple replay in our task requires direct experience and is not impacted by social observation.
source: Our data thus suggest that ripple replay in our task requires direct experience and is not impacted by social observation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the replay data.

claim: Introducing a rat to an open box induces no change or a small modification in CA1 place cell activities, but causes remapping of cells in the neighboring CA2 area.
source: Previous studies find that introducing a rat to an open box induces no change or a small modification in CA1 place cell activities, but causes remapping of cells in the neighboring CA2 area (von Heimendahl et al., 2012; Alexander et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The presence of a demonstrator per se would not dramatically alter place cell activities in the box.
source: However, the fact that consistent place cell patterns occur within rotation events in the box under all box conditions suggests that the presence of a demonstrator per se would not dramatically alter place cell activities in the box, consistent with these previous studies.
